content: The settings file is named prefs.js. The usual cause is being interrupted during shutdown by either an antivirus or VPN. Sometimes the file is read-only, in which case it's easy to fix. If you look in profile and see multiple prefs files, such as prefs-1.js, prefs-2.js, etc. that is further indication that thunderbird fails when shutting down. Although not a permanent fix, you can often restore the desired setting by removing all prefs files except the one with highest number, and renaming it to prefs.js. Repairing the cause is trial-and-error, again, usually an antivirus or VPN setting. That's all I know.

content:
You don't describe what you've done so far, and I don't understand what you mean by 'local folders being assigned a different ID.' I wonder if you have been making this more complicated than necessary. If you copy your entire Profile from the old installation to the new one, all your accounts, messages, folders, and preferences will transfer. Things will pickup pretty much pick up where they left off. There should be no need to "change the target address".

Here are some articles about the Profile and how to move it.

Move Thunderbird data to a new computer https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/moving-thunderbird-data-to-a-new-computer

Profiles - Where Thunderbird stores your messages and other user data backing up, restoring, moving https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/profiles-where-thunderbird-stores-user-data

And here is a good method to copy a profile to a new computer, courtesy of forum user david:

1) ensure thunderbird is NOT running on old machine 2) enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key 3) this should open windows file explorer in Appdata\roaming folder 4) highlight the Thunderbird folder and copy to external media 5) ensure thunderbird is installed on second computer, started once and NOT running 6) enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key 7) you should be in Appdata\roaming folder. DELETE the thunderbird folder there 8) now paste your copied thunderbird folder there. 9) start thunderbird and all should be there

content:
OK, that's good. I think what happened is that you deleted your profile, but you left the folder that contains the profiles. That folder has a file called PROFILES.INI that has a reference to your old profile name and location. Since it's not there any more Thunderbird complains.

To make it start up like a fresh install:

- Make sure Thunderbird is closed.

- Start up a Windows File Explorer window. In the Address Bar, type "%APPDATA% (no quotes, not case sensitive.) This opens the AppData folder, which contains personal settings for most of the programs on your computer.

- find the folder named "Thunderbird", Rename it to whatever you want - I suggest "Thunderbird.OLD".

When you next start Thunderbird, it should act like a fresh install and prompt you through the process of setting up an email account. Once you're satisfied that it's working the way you want, you can delete the Thunderbird.OLD folder.
